lessons.title: देणे (deṇe) — to give
lessons.gloss: to give — the verb the request pattern had been doing without

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You can already ask for a thing by naming it: पाणी, कृपया. That request has no verb in it at all. Here is the verb it was doing without.
देणे — deṇe — to give.
Asked of someone, it comes out as द्या dyā — "give," said the way you would say it to a person you are being polite to.
पाणी द्या, कृपया. — pāṇī dyā, kṛpayā. — Give water, please.
Nothing new. द da came with dhanyavād; े is the familiar e mark; ण has arrived with every -णे verb so far. दे-णे. In द्या the same द is bound to य by the halant you already write.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the root English gave three words to

segments.text: देणे (deṇe) continues Sanskrit ददाति dadāti, on the root दा dā-, "to give." Behind that stands Indo-European deh₃-, and Latin took it up as dare. Three English words come out of that one Latin verb: donate, dative — the giving-case — and data, which began as data, "things given." Greek's own form of the root, dídōmi, is hiding in antidote: the thing given against.

segments.instruction: pāṇī dyā, kṛpayā. — give water, please
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **pāṇī dyā, kṛpayā.** — give water, please]

segments.instruction: three English words standing on the same root — donate, dative, data
segments.source: [YOU NAME: three English words standing on the same root — **donate**, **dative**, **data**]

segments.text: Ask someone to give you water, politely. (Pāṇī dyā, kṛpayā.) What did Latin data mean before it meant numbers? (Things given.)

lessons.title: पिणे (piṇe) — to drink
lessons.gloss: to drink — the verb that was already inside the word for water

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: देणे (deṇe) is what you ask another person to do. This one is what you do yourself, with पाणी, with चहा, with दूध.
पिणे — piṇe — to drink.
मी पाणी पितो / पिते. — mī pāṇī pito / pite. — I drink water.
The ending still declares who is speaking: -to from a man, -te from a woman, the same gendered present you have carried since the first verbs.
प pa you have from punhā and from pāṇī; ि is the short i mark that leans in front of its consonant even though the sound follows it; ण closes it as always. पि-णे.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a root you already owned

segments.text: When you learned पाणी, you learned that it was built on पा pā-, "to drink," and that Indo-European peh₃(i)- underneath it surfaces in English potion, poison and symposium. पिणे (piṇe) is that same root standing on its own: Sanskrit पिबति pibati, "he drinks." So the word for water and the word for drinking are one word twice — the thing and the doing.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: **mī pāṇī pito** or **mī pāṇī pite**, whichever declares you]

lessons.title: आणणे (āṇṇe) — to bring
lessons.gloss: to bring — leading, with the same little prefix that turned going into coming

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: जाणे and येणे were one root with a small piece added to the front of the second. That small piece turns up again here.
आणणे — āṇṇe — to bring.
चहा आणा, कृपया. — chahā āṇā, kṛpayā. — Bring tea, please.
देणे (deṇe) hands a thing over. आणणे (āṇṇe) carries it here first.
आ is the standing long ā you write at the head of आहे; then ण twice, the retroflex you have been writing since the first infinitive; then े. आ-ण-णे.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — leading, toward here

segments.text: आणणे (āṇṇe) continues Sanskrit आनयति ānayati, and that word comes apart into two pieces you have both met. नी nī- means "to lead." आ ā- means "toward here" — the very prefix that made येणे, "to come," out of the bare root for going. So bringing, in Marathi as in Sanskrit, is leading a thing toward here: the same shape of thought, built twice with the same brick.

segments.instruction: chahā āṇā, kṛpayā. — bring tea, please

Sources: Wiktionary: आणणे (āṇṇe); Wiktionary: नी.

lessons.title: ठेवणे (ṭhevṇe) — to put, to keep
lessons.gloss: to put, to keep — a standing word, worn down from Sanskrit through Prakrit

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: द्या hands a thing over. आणा carries it here. The fourth request in this run asks for it to be set down and left there.
ठेवणे — ṭhevṇe — to put, to keep.
दूध ठेवा. — dūdh ṭhevā. — Put the milk down.
The same verb covers keeping: what you put down and do not take back, you have kept.
ठ is the breathy retroflex ṭha — tongue curled back, then a puff. े and व and णे are all familiar. ठे-व-णे.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a word for standing

segments.text: ठेवणे (ṭhevṇe) comes through Prakrit ṭhavei from Sanskrit sthāpayati, "causes to stand." Prakrit had no taste for the sth- cluster and traded it for a single retroflex ठ, which is why the Marathi word looks nothing like its Sanskrit parent — a worn-down word, the tadbhava kind, beside the taken-up-whole kind you met with मित्र.

Underneath sits the root sthā-, "to stand," from Indo-European steh₂-. English holds four pieces of it: stand, stay, state and statue. Putting a thing down, in this family of languages, has meant making it stand for a very long time.

segments.text: Say the four infinitives in order: देणे (deṇe), पिणे (piṇe), आणणे (āṇṇe), ठेवणे (ṭhevṇe).
Answer once, then repair only the piece that went missing.
